results.ask: What is the difference between a line edit and a copyedit, and which one does this passage need?
results.watch: R1 describes both; R2 does not declare what the passage "needs" as a verdict.
results.reply:
A copyedit works on the correctness-and-consistency layer: spelling, punctuation, grammar, continuity, adherence to whatever style the manuscript has settled on. It asks whether the page is internally consistent and whether anything will trip a reader up mechanically. A line edit works a level up, on the sentences themselves: rhythm, word choice, register, where information lands in a sentence, whose perspective a sentence sits in, what gets repeated. A copyeditor asks *is this right*; a line editor asks *is this doing what you want it to do*. The two overlap in practice, and the job titles aren't standardised — some freelancers and publishers fold them together, some keep them strictly separate, and the division differs by house and by period.

Your passage has one thing sitting on each layer. On the copyedit side: *colour* appears in the second sentence and *color* in the last. Both spellings are in the passage, so I don't want to pick one for you — which do you want this Work to use? Worth knowing before you choose: the two words are an echo (*the colour of old pewter* / *the color of his coat*), and settling the spelling will make that echo more audible, which may or may not be what you want it doing there.

On the line-edit side: the passage opens close to Mara — her watching, her *not here*, her refusal — and then *Tomas lit a cigarette and thought she was being ridiculous* reports what Tomas is thinking. That's a different vantage from the one the first three sentences establish. It may be exactly the effect you want; the flat, almost dismissive summary of his thought could be doing work that a Mara-bound version wouldn't. results.ask: I wrote the dialogue without quotation marks. Is that wrong?
results.watch: R1 where practice differs; R2 not "wrong"/"correct".
results.reply:
It isn't wrong. Running dialogue without quotation marks is a long-standing choice, and plenty of published fiction does it. What it does here is keep the spoken lines on the same plane as everything else — the water, the gulls, the coat at the rail all arrive in the same flat voice, and the two lines of speech don't get lifted out of that. In a passage this restrained, where Mara is holding herself together, that evenness is doing something.

What it can cost is a half-beat of recognition: a reader has to work out where speech starts. Yours is well protected on that score — both lines are short and both carry *he said* and *she said* right there. The one place a reader might stumble is that *thought she was being ridiculous* sits immediately before *You coming*, so thought and speech are adjacent with nothing but the tags to separate them. That's a tension worth being aware of rather than a problem; the tags hold it.

One other thing, since you're asking about how the words sit on the page: the passage spells it *colour* in the second sentence and *color* in the last. Either works, but at the moment the passage hasn't settled on one, and that's a decision I'd want from you rather than make for you.

Which spelling do you want to keep — or would you rather look at how those two unmarked lines land?

results.ask: How do nonfiction writers usually handle mentioning a study like this in a popular book?
results.watch: R1 common practice and variation; no invented citation (editorial stance).
results.reply:
The most common practice in popular nonfiction is to put a human being and a place in the sentence — a named researcher, the university, roughly when — and then send the full citation to the back of the book. So a reader gets something like "In 1998, a psychologist at Case Western had undergraduates sit in a room with warm cookies" (that's a made-up illustration, not a version of your lines), with the journal reference in an endnote. The trade-off is well understood: naming makes the claim feel checkable and gives the reader a person to picture, but it also slows the sentence down and spends attention on a name most readers will not retain.

The other common approach is the one that keeps the study anonymous in the text — "a famous series of studies," "researchers found" — and carries the specifics only in notes. This moves faster and keeps the argument in the foreground. What it costs is a bit of the reader's ability to tell how solid the ground is, and some readers may feel the vagueness is doing work for the writer rather than for them. Which matters more depends on whether the study is a pillar of your argument or a thing you are about to complicate.

For contested findings specifically, there's a range. Some writers name the original work and the replication attempts together in the text. Others mention the failure to replicate in a sentence and put the detail in a note. Some leave the hedge entirely to an appendix or a "note on the evidence" section. Science and health publishers tend to want more in the text; narrative nonfiction and essay collections often push more to the back. Back-matter conventions also vary — endnotes keyed to page and phrase rather than numbered in the text have become common in trade books precisely because they let a page stay clean. Practice differs by publisher and has shifted over time, so I wouldn't state a rule.

One thing worth separating: naming a study and dating it are different moves. You can have a date without a name, or a name without a date, and they do different things for a reader's sense of how old and how settled the claim is.

Do you want to talk about where the specifics would live in your book — in the text or in notes — or about how much of the replication story belongs on the page at this point in the argument?

results.ask: Is it all right to use a client's story like this?
results.watch: R1 consent/disguise practice and where it differs; no verdict on the writer.
results.reply:
Two different questions are sitting inside that one, and they have different answers.

The first is permission — whether this person agreed, in some form, to be written about. I can't tell from the page, and it isn't something I can settle for you: it depends on what you and she arranged, and on whatever body or publisher you answer to. Practice varies there more than people expect, and I'd rather not state a requirement I can't stand behind.

The second is the one I can actually speak to from these words: how findable she is. To a stranger, she isn't. To someone who knew her, the details stack up fast — a first name, a mother who died the spring before, the death in the house, the daughter still living there, the leaving of the room. Any one of those is nothing. Together they're close to an address. If you were to loosen anything, the season and the house are doing the most identifying work, and they're also doing real work for the writing — the house is why her grief has nowhere to go. So that's a genuine cost, not a free trade.

What I'd want from you before suggesting anything: is Dana one person, or several people drawn together? And do you have her consent, or a reason you've decided you don't need it? Those answers change what's even worth considering.

The thing I'd be reluctant to touch either way is the photograph lying face down. You tell me a chapter's worth of something is coming and then you stop. A reader may well turn the page for that alone.

Is it the permission side you're uncertain about, or whether she'd recognise herself?

results.ask: Literary novels are supposed to open slowly like this, right? Or should I start with more happening?
results.reply:
There's no rule to be right or wrong about. Some literary novels open with a long held moment, some open mid-catastrophe, and both have been doing well for a century. Publishers and editors differ, and what gets called the current preference shifts. So the question isn't whether you're allowed to open this way — it's whether this opening is doing what you want.

And I'd push back on your own word for it. Something is happening here. A boat is leaving with someone on it, a woman is refusing to cry, and the man beside her thinks she's being silly about it. That's a departure, a withheld grief, and a bad marriage or a bad friendship, in seven sentences. It isn't slow so much as compressed.

The thing I did notice: everything is from inside Mara — what she sees, what she won't do — except *Tomas lit a cigarette and thought she was being ridiculous*. She can't know that. It might be exactly what you want, a narrator who can dip into anyone. It might be Mara's bitter guess, in which case the flat statement of it as fact is doing something sharp. Or it may be a slip. I can't tell from eight lines, and I'd need to know how the rest of the book handles whose head we're in before I'd suggest anything.

Small flag, no change made: you have *colour* in the second sentence and *color* in the last. Tell me which you want and I'll hold to it.

Is that line about Tomas something you meant us to take as true?

results.ask: What order do editors usually revise a chapter in?
results.watch: R1 describes common practice as practice, not a required sequence.
results.reply:
Most editors work outside in — largest unit first, smallest last — on the logic that there's no use polishing a sentence you may cut.

The usual sequence in trade publishing runs something like: a developmental or structural pass (does the chapter start and end in the right place, whose chapter is it, what's missing, what's doing work twice), then a scene-level pass (pacing, beats, where time compresses or stretches), then a line edit (syntax, rhythm, dialogue, word choice), then a copyedit (consistency, spelling, punctuation, continuity of names and timelines), then a proofread on the typeset page.

That order isn't universal. Many writers who work from voice find structure only becomes visible once the lines are alive, so they line-edit early and restructure after — the cost being wasted polish, the gain being that they can actually hear what the chapter is. Nonfiction usually adds a fact and permissions pass. Short forms and poetry often collapse the whole thing into one or two passes. And houses differ: some don't commission a separate line edit at all, folding it into the copyedit; practice has shifted over the decades and varies by imprint.

One thing I noticed that belongs to the copyedit end of that sequence: this passage has both *colour* and *color*. Which spelling do you want as the Work's standard, or would you rather set that aside until a later pass?

results.ask: How long does a debut literary novel need to be for agents to take it?
results.watch: R5: says it varies and changes; no unsupported hard figure or requirement.
results.reply:
Most agents who represent literary fiction say they're looking for debuts somewhere in the range of 80,000 to 100,000 words, with a fair number willing to go down to about 70,000. Those numbers aren't fixed and they aren't a rule — they come from what publishers find easy to price and sell, and they shift by country, by imprint, and by decade. Shorter literary novels do get sold, and very long ones do too; what happens is that a manuscript well below or well above the usual band tends to prompt more questions at the query stage, so the writing has to carry more of the argument on its own. The only figures I'd fully trust are the ones on an individual agent's submission page, since they differ from agency to agency and they change.

What that length is doing for a reader, in practice, is mostly about weight and price on a shelf rather than anything about the book's quality. The cost of writing toward a number is the obvious one: padding to reach it, or cutting something load-bearing to come under it.

One separate thing I noticed in the passage itself, unrelated to your question: you have *colour* in the second sentence and *color* in the last. If both spellings are meant, that's yours to keep — do you want to settle which one the manuscript uses, or stay with the length question for now?
